What is student growth?

Terminology
• Achievement: A point in time measure/indication of what a student
 knows and can do. Also referred to as status, attainment. Reported as
 a scaled score, percentile
• Growth: The “change” in the level of achievement associated with an
 individual student measure at least two points in time.
• Improvement: The “change” in the level of achievement associated
 with two groups of students formed by school or demographic
 groups (e.g., 2024 versus 2025 outcomes for Grade 4 students in a
 given school). This is the most common metric of change.
• Not all change is “growth”. There are different types of changes and

Why Student Growth?
 If you care about student achievement,
 then you care about student growth.

• Where you are is a function of where
 you started and how quickly you’ve
 travelled since.
• Student growth and student
 attainment/achievement are related

• Those who start behind tend to

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• There are 3 general approaches of calculating student
 growth:
 • Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
 • Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
 • Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Growth as an amount of change:
 • What could be more simple?
 • Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
 • Requires a vertical scale (which ERB has)
 • Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
 • Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions
 • Interpreting change requires context.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
•This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
•Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
•Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to
 acquire that context.
 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age and is
 shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4
 inches—is a well understood quantity that any parent can grasp
 and calculate at home using a simple yardstick. However, parents
 leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing only how much their
 child has grown would likely be wanting for more information:
 Parents are not interested in an absolute magnitude of growth, but
 instead in a norm-referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase
 alongside the height increases of similar children. 12

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student with similar
 characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students with (at
 least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for stakeholders to
 understand student growth.
• The ERB SGP Model creates growth norms for all students using regression (i.e.,
 peer-based) analyses.
• These norms allow stakeholders to understand what an ambitious yet
 reasonable expectation is for each student.

What is a student growth percentile
(SGP)?

 14

Student Growth Percentiles
• Research on the SGP model began in 2007.
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model was extended
 to include a criterion-referenced component.
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state reporting and
 accountability systems occurred in subsequent years and student growth
 became more common across state assessment systems.
• Goal or the model is to create an individual level growth metric that is
 informative to different stakeholders ranging from parents to policy
 makers.
• Currently, more than two dozen states and several assessment
 organizations use SGPs for diagnostic and accountability purposes.
 15

Student Growth Percentiles
• Different growth models answer different questions.
• Different stakeholder groups ask different questions.
• Parents are most concerned about how their child is doing.
• To effectively engage parents and communities in a productive conversation
 about student learning (i.e. growth), a growth model should describe:
 • What is? How much are students learning/growing.
 • What should be? How much would we like students to grow/learn.
 • What is reasonable? How much is it reasonable to expect students to grow/
 learn.
• Most other growth models do not provide a student level metric. They provide a
 school summary used for accountability purposes.

Growth Model: Other Options
• Almost all current growth model use large amounts of data to
 create “norms” against which student growth is judged.
• Growth models utilize various forms of regression to adjust
 for initial student achievement (and, in some instances) other
 demographic characteristics.
• Other growth models include value-added models, value-
 table models

Properties of SGP growth
• All students regardless of starting place can have high or low growth — growth is uncorrelated with prior achievement.
• Growth is uncorrelated from year-to-year. High growth one year doesn’t indicate growth in the following year.
• Growth analyses do not include demographic adjustments. Growth differs for different demographic subgroups.
 • Growth by ethnicity ranges from a median SGP of low 40s to high 50s (depending upon grade and content area)
 • Economically disadvantaged students have median SGP in mid to low 40s (depending upon grade and content area)
 • Special needs students have median SGP in low 40s (depending upon grade and content area)

• Included the calculation of student growth percentiles and student growth projections
 (which provide SGTs).
• When New Jersey transitioned to PARCC, NJ received both state and consortium normed .

Differential Impact versus Bias
• Differences in growth results (differential impact) do not necessarily constitute bias.
• The measure can show differences without necessarily being “biased”
• However, differential impact, particularly when used for accountability, can be VERY
 thorny issue.
• I advocate for distinguishing between the MEASURE (e.g., status, growth, …) and the
 EVALUATION done with the measure:
 • The evaluation may involve adjustments for circumstances.
 • Those adjustments don’t need to be baked into the measure.
